stories.headline: Trump's Nvidia intervention: pardon talk, board U-turn, governance questions
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump publicly backed Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, 11 days after Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, one involving a person suspected of being a Chinese spy. Trump said a pardon for Huang is 'always an option' but likely would not be needed, and urged him to testify truthfully before Congress rather than plead the Fifth. Nvidia's board reversed its earlier position under reported pressure from the White House and Huang's influential backers, while the US attorney general declined to answer questions about an Nvidia investigation. Nvidia's share price fell about 7% as lawmakers demanded answers, and reports estimate Trump may have gained up to $15 million on Nvidia shares after Huang's return. The episode has triggered debate over board independence, CEO accountability and political influence over strategically vital technology firms.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live case study on corporate governance, board independence and political interference in private firms, set against the US-China contest over AI chips and semiconductor supply chains.

perspectives.take: Indian business daily frames it as presidential pressure on Nvidia's board, with Trump linking a possible pardon to Huang's testimony before Congress.

Indian business daily stresses that the board was no match for Trump and Huang's powerful backers, and separately flags Trump's reported personal share gains and his claim that China could have hired Huang.
UK public broadcaster centres on accountability — the attorney general dodging questions on the Nvidia investigation and the 7% share-price fall amid lawmaker demands.
Indian daily characterises the episode as an extraordinary presidential intervention in the leadership of a private company.
Focuses on the governance debate — what checks exist on a powerful chief executive after a contested reinstatement.
Academic explainer shifts the lens to technology, explaining what AI chips are and why Nvidia's chips sit at the centre of the AI boom and US-China competition.
US tabloid, exclusive framing — plays up the pardon remark and Trump's advice to Huang not to plead the Fifth before Congress.
US cable network downplays the pardon angle, reporting Trump calls it 'always an option' but says it likely won't be needed.

static.topic: Corporate governance and board independence
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Corporate Governance & Regulation
static.whatIsIt: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, balancing the interests of shareholders, management, employees and the wider public. Board independence — directors free of promoter or executive influence — is its central safeguard.
static.background: India's framework rests on the Companies Act, 2013 (independent directors, audit committees, related-party transaction rules) and SEBI's LODR Regulations, 2015, which followed the Kumarmangalam Birla Committee (1999) and the Satyam fraud (2009). The Kotak Committee (2017) strengthened board and disclosure norms, and SEBI has since required separation of the chairperson and MD/CEO roles for the largest listed companies.
static.socioEconomic: Concentrated promoter ownership in Indian listed firms, and the dominance of a few large technology firms globally, both weaken board checks; governance failures erode retail investor confidence and household savings.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's board reversed its decision on CEO Jensen Huang within 11 days under reported pressure from US President Donald Trump and Huang's backers, prompting debate on whether boards can resist powerful executives and political pressure.
static.wayForward: Strengthen independent director selection and tenure, enforce stricter disclosure of political and related-party dealings, and insulate regulators from executive interference.
prelimsPointers: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992.
The Companies Act, 2013 requires every listed public company to have at least one-third of its directors as independent directors.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether regulatory and board-level checks in India are adequate to hold dominant promoters and CEOs accountable, in light of global episodes of political interference in corporate leadership.

static.topic: Semiconductors and India's chip ambitions
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Industry & Infrastructure; Science & Technology
static.whatIsIt: Semiconductors are the foundational input for electronics, computing and AI hardware. Advanced AI accelerators such as GPUs are designed by firms like Nvidia and fabricated in a handful of global foundries.
static.background: India launched the India Semiconductor Mission in December 2021 with a ₹76,000 crore outlay under the programme for development of semiconductors and display manufacturing ecosystems, offering fiscal support for fabrication, ATMP/OSAT and display units. The Design Linked Incentive scheme supports fabless design startups. In 2024 the government approved India's first set of semiconductor units, including a fabrication plant in Gujarat and assembly-test units in Assam and Gujarat.
static.geography: Chip fabrication is concentrated in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the US and China; India is building capacity in Gujarat and Assam.
static.socioEconomic: Semiconductors underpin the electronics, automotive and defence sectors; domestic fabrication reduces import dependence and creates high-skill jobs, but needs large capital, water and uninterrupted power.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's centrality to the AI boom, and the US-China contest over advanced chips, form the backdrop to the political storm over CEO Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement.
static.wayForward: Sustained capital and skilling, reliable utilities, and technology-transfer partnerships; India should target mature-node fabrication and packaging segments first.
prelimsPointers: India Semiconductor Mission was launched in December 2021 with a ₹76,000 crore outlay.
ATMP stands for Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging — the back-end of chip manufacturing.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's semiconductor mission can reduce supply-chain vulnerability while competing in a global market dominated by a few firms and shaped by geopolitically contested export controls.

static.topic: US–China technology rivalry and export controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance & Technology Geopolitics
static.whatIsIt: The US and China compete for leadership in AI, semiconductors and advanced computing. The US uses export controls, entity listings and investment screening to restrict China's access to advanced chips and chipmaking tools.
static.background: US export controls on advanced computing chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment were tightened from October 2022 onwards, with further rounds covering high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking tools. China responded with domestic substitution programmes and export curbs on critical minerals such as gallium and germanium in 2023.
static.geography: Supply chains run through Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and the Netherlands, making the contest a genuinely global one.
static.socioEconomic: Export controls raise costs and fragment supply chains, affecting consumer electronics, AI services and developing economies that depend on affordable computing.
static.whyInNews: Trump defended Huang's return by claiming China could have hired him, underlining how AI-chip leadership is now treated as a national-security issue in Washington.
static.wayForward: India should pursue technology partnerships and domestic capability while advocating predictable, rules-based trade in critical technologies.
prelimsPointers: The US CHIPS and Science Act (2022) provides subsidies for domestic semiconductor manufacturing.
China imposed export controls on gallium and germanium in 2023; both are critical inputs for semiconductors.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how US–China technological decoupling affects India's strategic autonomy, supply chains and semiconductor ambitions.

stories.headline: COP31 in Antalya closes without a pact; food, forest and ocean outcomes agreed
stories.summary: The COP31 climate talks, held in Antalya, Turkey, closed without agreement on an overarching political "pact", even though negotiators did reach outcomes covering food, forests, oceans and nature. Carbon Brief's team, in a post-summit live session, walked through what the final texts did and did not deliver, and where the gaps remain. The absence of a headline pact means the conference's substantive results sit in sectoral and thematic decisions rather than in a single consolidated political declaration. For India, the outcome matters because sectoral decisions on land, food systems and forests intersect directly with its NDC targets, its forestry and biodiversity commitments, and its stance on equity and climate finance.
stories.whyItMatters: COP outcomes shape the UNFCCC negotiating trajectory that India's NDCs, forestry and biodiversity policy must align with — a recurring GS-III environment and GS-II global governance theme.

perspectives.take: Its live post-COP31 discussion frames the summit as one where the headline political moment was missing, with journalists fielding questions on what the absence of a pact means for the wider climate process.
Its outcomes explainer focuses on the thematic wins — food, forests, oceans and nature — treating these sectoral decisions as the substantive legacy of Antalya despite the failed pact.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. The Paris Agreement uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps constrain developing-country mitigation and adaptation, making equity a persistent negotiating fault line.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya closed without an overarching pact, leaving sectoral decisions on food, forests, oceans and nature as the summit's main outputs.
static.wayForward: Strengthen sectoral implementation under the UNFCCC while pressing for predictable climate finance and clear technology-transfer pathways consistent with CBDR-RC.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
static.mainsAngle: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps; examine equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: Biodiversity, Wetlands & Conservation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity & Conservation
static.whatIsIt: India is one of 17 megadiverse countries. Key instruments: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Biological Diversity Act 2002, Forest Conservation Act 1980, and the CBD (1992) with its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).
static.background: The Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands; India has 80+ Ramsar sites. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation. The 30x30 target aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
static.geography: India's four recognised biodiversity hotspots — Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland/Nicobar — span forest, coastal and island ecosystems.
static.socioEconomic: Conservation must be balanced against forest-dependent community rights under the Forest Rights Act and against human-wildlife conflict pressures.
static.whyInNews: COP31 produced agreed outcomes on forests, oceans and nature, linking the climate negotiations directly to biodiversity and ecosystem governance.
static.wayForward: Integrate climate and biodiversity goals domestically through ecosystem restoration, wetland protection and community-led conservation, tracking progress against the 30x30 target.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar.
World Wetlands Day: 2 February.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing conservation with development and community rights (FRA); human-wildlife conflict management.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: COP31's failure to adopt a pact illustrates the recurring difficulty of consensus-based multilateral outcomes, a pattern relevant to wider UN reform debates.
static.wayForward: Push for reformed, representative multilateral processes — including UNSC expansion — so that consensus-based bodies remain effective on cross-border challenges such as climate change.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles (veto politics, Africa's Ezulwini Consensus).

prelims: COP31 was hosted in Antalya, Turkey, and concluded without an overarching political pact.
Despite the missing pact, the summit agreed outcomes on food, forests, oceans and nature.
The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent climate treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it.
India's climate commitments include net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
stories.mainsQuestion: The absence of a headline political pact at COP31, alongside agreed sectoral outcomes on food, forests, oceans and nature, raises questions about the effectiveness of consensus-based climate multilateralism. Examine this in the light of India's climate commitments and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities.

stories.headline: US weighs fresh import duties on India, China and 14 trading partners
stories.summary: Washington is reported to be preparing a fresh wave of import duties covering India, China and 14 other trading partners, with the decision potentially coming within the week. Tariff rates, product coverage and possible exemptions are still undetermined, and China is said to face the steepest proposed rates. If imposed, the duties would sit on top of existing trade barriers and add fresh uncertainty for exporters in the affected economies, including India. The reports are based on unnamed official sources, and the final scope will depend on the outcome of the administration's internal review.
stories.whyItMatters: Unilateral tariff action by the US directly affects India's export earnings and the credibility of the rules-based multilateral trading system. It is a recurring theme in GS-II India–US relations and GS-III external-sector and trade-policy questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the move as an incremental addition to existing trade barriers, stressing that rates and exemptions are undetermined — measured business-desk tone, no political attribution.

static.topic: US–India Trade Relations and Tariff Frictions
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral relations with major powers (United States); India and the global economy
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral economic relationship covering merchandise and services trade, market access, tariff and non-tariff barriers, and periodic negotiation tracks such as the India–US Trade Policy Forum.
static.background: India–US economic engagement expanded after the 1991 reforms. In 2018 the US imposed Section 232 duties on steel and aluminium imports, including from India; India responded in 2019 with retaliatory tariffs on select US products. The US withdrew Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) benefits for India in June 2019. Both sides have since pursued limited trade packages and resumed discussions under the Trade Policy Forum.
static.geography: The US is India's largest single-country goods export destination; bilateral trade is concentrated in pharmaceuticals, gems and jewellery, textiles, engineering goods and energy.
static.socioEconomic: Tariff changes affect exporter margins, labour-intensive MSME clusters in India, and consumer prices in the importing country; market concentration increases vulnerability to a single partner's action.
static.whyInNews: Washington is reported to be weighing a fresh wave of import duties covering India, China and 14 other trading partners.
static.wayForward: Pursue negotiated market-access packages, diversify export destinations, strengthen domestic trade-remedy capacity, and use WTO dispute settlement where feasible.
prelimsPointers: The US withdrew GSP benefits for India in June 2019.
India imposed retaliatory tariffs on select US products in 2019 following US steel and aluminium duties.
The US is India's largest single-country goods export destination.
static.mainsAngle: How should India balance bilateral negotiation with multilateral rules when major trading partners resort to unilateral tariff action?

static.topic: WTO Tariff Architecture: MFN, Bound Rates and Trade Remedies
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External sector; international trade institutions and rules
static.whatIsIt: The WTO framework disciplining tariffs: MFN treatment, bound tariff commitments in members' schedules, national treatment, and permitted contingent measures such as anti-dumping, countervailing and safeguard duties.
static.background: GATT 1947 laid down the basic disciplines; the WTO was established in 1995 after the Uruguay Round. Dispute settlement runs through panels and the Appellate Body, whose appointments have been blocked since 2019, leaving the system partly paralysed and pushing members towards unilateral measures and interim appeal arrangements.
static.socioEconomic: Tariff predictability underpins global value chains; unilateral duties raise import costs, invite retaliation and fragment production networks.
static.whyInNews: Fresh US tariff proposals targeting India, China and other partners revive questions about the boundary between domestic trade law and WTO commitments.
static.wayForward: Reform WTO dispute settlement, conclude pending negotiations on fisheries subsidies and e-commerce, and strengthen plurilateral and regional cooperation as a complement to multilateral rules.
prelimsPointers: MFN requires a WTO member to extend the same trade advantages it gives one member to all members.
Bound tariffs are ceilings committed in a member's schedule; applied tariffs may be lower.
The WTO Appellate Body has been unable to hear new appeals since December 2019.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether the WTO's tariff and dispute-settlement architecture can effectively restrain unilateral trade measures by major economies.

static.topic: India's Export Competitiveness and Market Diversification
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External sector; exports, industrial policy and Make in India
static.whatIsIt: India's strategy to expand and diversify merchandise and services exports, reduce dependence on a few markets, and improve logistics, quality infrastructure and tariff competitiveness.
static.background: Post-1991 liberalisation shifted India towards an outward-oriented trade regime; successive Foreign Trade Policy documents set multi-year export goals. Recent years saw emphasis on production-linked incentive schemes, free trade agreements with the UAE and Australia (both in force from 2022), the EFTA agreement (2024), and efforts towards rupee-based trade settlement.
static.geography: Principal markets include the US, EU, UAE, China and Singapore; major export categories are petroleum products, gems and jewellery, pharmaceuticals, electronics and engineering goods.
static.socioEconomic: Export-linked employment is concentrated in labour-intensive MSME clusters, so tariff shocks in a major market transmit quickly to incomes and employment.
static.whyInNews: Proposed US duties add to pressure on Indian exporters already facing uncertain global demand.
static.wayForward: Conclude and implement FTAs, strengthen export credit and logistics, upgrade quality and testing infrastructure, and deepen domestic value addition to reduce exposure to any single market.
prelimsPointers: The India–UAE CEPA and the India–Australia ECTA both came into force in 2022.
Petroleum products, gems and jewellery, and pharmaceuticals are among India's largest export categories.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how trade-policy uncertainty in major markets should shape India's export diversification strategy and industrial policy.

prelims: The US has historically used Section 301 (against China) and Section 232 (steel and aluminium) to impose tariffs outside the ordinary WTO tariff schedule.
Under WTO rules, MFN treatment requires non-discriminatory tariffs among members, subject to each member's bound tariff ceilings.
GSP benefits extended by the US to India lapsed in June 2019.
The US is India's largest single-country goods export destination, making Indian exporters directly sensitive to US tariff decisions.
stories.mainsQuestion: Unilateral tariff actions by major economies are increasingly testing the rules-based multilateral trading system. Examine the implications for India's external sector and suggest a calibrated response strategy.

stories.headline: Russia strikes Zaporizhzhia; Ukraine hits Russian warship in Libya
stories.summary: A Russian overnight strike on Zaporizhzhia in southern Ukraine killed two civilians and wounded 48 people, among them four children, according to Ukrainian officials. The attack came days after Ukrainian forces hit a Russian warship docked at a naval base in Libya — an operation President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly welcomed, signalling the war's reach beyond the Black Sea. Russian President Vladimir Putin separately accused Ukraine of striking Russian oil plants despite appeals from US President Donald Trump, and promised retaliation. Reporting by Mint adds a quieter dimension: recruitment networks offering signing bonuses of up to $35,000 and promised monthly incomes of $3,000 are drawing men from Indonesia and the Philippines into jobs advertised as logistics, security and construction that feed Russia's war effort.
stories.whyItMatters: The story ties together three recurring UPSC themes — the paralysis of UN collective security, energy infrastructure as an instrument of war, and the transnational labour migration that sustains a war economy. It also shows how a European conflict now produces security, energy and migration externalities across Africa and Asia.

perspectives.take: Leads with the civilian toll in Zaporizhzhia (two dead, 48 wounded, including four children) and frames Kyiv's Libya operation as an explanation Ukraine felt compelled to offer.
Carries the Kremlin line — Putin's claim that Ukraine hit Russian oil plants despite Trump's requests, plus a promise of retaliation; sourcing leans on Russian presidential statements.
Centres on Zelenskyy's public praise for the strike on a Russian warship docked at a Libyan naval base, emphasising Ukraine's ability to project force far from its own territory.
Shifts the lens to the labour supply side — how large signing bonuses and wage promises pull Indonesian and Filipino men into roles advertised as logistics, security and construction.
US wire-style report pairing the Zaporizhzhia casualty figures with Kyiv's account of the Libya attack, without independent verification of either claim.
Frames the Zaporizhzhia strike by its timing — 'days after' the ship attack off Libya — foregrounding the escalation cycle rather than either single event.
Regional US outlet running the same casualty story with headline emphasis on wounded children, a more human-interest framing.

static.topic: UN Security Council and the Russia-Ukraine War
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance / United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council (UNSC) holds primary responsibility for international peace and security. It has 15 members — five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. Action on the Russia-Ukraine war has repeatedly been blocked by the veto of a P5 member that is itself a party to the conflict.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 with six principal organs. India is a founding member and one of the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for permanent UNSC expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: Russia's strike on Zaporizhzhia and Ukraine's strike on a Russian warship docked in Libya illustrate how the conflict has spread geographically, even as the UNSC remains unable to act because of P5 veto politics.
static.wayForward: Move the IGN towards text-based negotiations, build coalitions around the African Common Position (Ezulwini Consensus) and keep pressing for expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits in The Hague; UN Headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent membership rests on representativeness, population and contributions to peacekeeping; assess the obstacles posed by veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: Labour Migration into a War Economy
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Inclusive Growth & Employment / Labour Migration
static.whatIsIt: The recruitment of foreign nationals into military-linked and war-support work, and the measurement of employment and deprivation in sending countries. Poverty is tracked through NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and consumption surveys; employment through the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
static.background: NITI Aayog's National MPI (2021) uses 12 indicators across health, education and living standards. PLFS has reported quarterly urban and annual all-India data since 2017. India became the world's most populous country in 2023, making its labour mobility a globally significant phenomenon.
static.geography: Sending countries named in reporting include Indonesia and the Philippines; the destination is Russia.
static.socioEconomic: Signing bonuses reported at up to $35,000 and promised monthly incomes of about $3,000 draw workers into jobs advertised as logistics, security and construction — a wage gap that makes risky overseas recruitment attractive in lower-income Asian economies.
static.whyInNews: A Mint report describes how Russia's war machine draws in Asian workers through such advertisements, raising questions of informed consent, consular protection and regulation of overseas recruitment.
static.wayForward: Strengthen bilateral labour mobility agreements, regulate recruitment agents, mandate pre-departure orientation and ensure consular access for workers in conflict zones.
prelimsPointers: MPI dimensions: health, education and standard of living (3 dimensions, 12 indicators).
Unemployment Rate = unemployed / labour force.
static.mainsAngle: Quality of employment, structural transformation and the skills gap — examine how overseas labour migration interacts with domestic employment outcomes.

static.topic: Energy Infrastructure as a Target in the Russia-Ukraine War
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Energy Security / Infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: Refineries, oil plants and export terminals have become recurring targets in the war, turning energy infrastructure into both a military objective and a lever on global oil markets. For import-dependent economies such as India, such strikes transmit directly into the import bill, inflation and the current account.
static.background: Since the full-scale invasion of 2022, energy infrastructure has repeatedly featured as a target, while sanctions and price-cap measures have redirected Russian crude flows towards Asian buyers. Global oil markets have repeatedly repriced on supply-disruption news.
static.geography: Russian refining and export infrastructure; Black Sea and Mediterranean shipping routes; Libya's naval facilities.
static.socioEconomic: Oil price volatility affects India's import bill, retail inflation, the fiscal cost of fuel subsidies and the current account deficit.
static.whyInNews: Putin said Ukraine struck Russian oil plants despite US President Donald Trump's requests, and promised retaliation — signalling further risk to energy infrastructure.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude import sources, expand strategic petroleum reserves, accelerate renewables and efficiency to blunt price shocks.
prelimsPointers: India is among the world's largest crude oil importers and meets the bulk of its requirement through imports.
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserve sites are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.

stories.headline: BJP and SAD reunite for Punjab polls, reshaping the contest
stories.summary: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the BJP have come together again to contest the upcoming Punjab Assembly elections, ending a period of separation that began when the SAD walked out of the NDA over the three farm laws. Reporting indicates the reunion was pushed at the highest level of the BJP leadership, with the party presenting it as a step towards Punjab's prosperity. Farmer leaders have attacked the tie-up as 'highly dangerous' for the state, keeping alive the alliance's unresolved baggage from the 2020-21 farm agitation. Commentators argue that a united SAD-BJP front could consolidate non-AAP, non-Congress votes, whereas the two parties contesting separately would have split the same opposition space. The harder tasks — seat-sharing, reconciling cadres and managing the farm-law legacy — are only now beginning.
stories.whyItMatters: Pre-poll alliances decide vote transfer, seat arithmetic and the shape of opposition space in a key border state, making this a live case study in coalition politics and agrarian pressure-group politics for GS-II and GS-III.

perspectives.take: Frames the reunion as restoring both parties to contention: had they fought separately they would have split the opposition space, leaving AAP and the Congress as the principal rivals.

A regional paper with deep Punjab coverage that carries both sides — farmer leaders calling the alliance 'highly dangerous' for Punjab, BJP leader Kewal Dhillon calling it a step for Punjab's prosperity, and reporting that PM Modi pushed for the tie-up.

static.topic: Coalition politics and pre-poll alliances in India
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Political Parties, Elections and Coalition Politics
static.whatIsIt: A pre-poll alliance is an arrangement between two or more parties to contest an election on a shared seat-sharing formula and a common campaign, so that their vote banks transfer to each other's candidates and anti-incumbency is consolidated rather than split.
static.background: India's coalition era began in earnest with the National Front government of 1989, followed by the NDA (1998) and UPA (2004) formations at the Centre. In Punjab, the SAD and the BJP have a long history of alliance, governing the state together in the late 1990s and again from 2007 to 2012; the SAD exited the NDA in 2020 over the three farm laws, and the two are now reuniting for the coming Assembly polls.
static.geography: Punjab is a north-western border state with 13 Lok Sabha seats and a 117-member Legislative Assembly.
static.socioEconomic: Punjab's politics is shaped by an agrarian economy, strong farmer unions, a large Sikh electorate and a history of regional-party dominance, all of which make alliance arithmetic unusually sensitive.
static.whyInNews: The SAD and the BJP have announced a pre-poll alliance for the Punjab Assembly elections, a reunion that reshapes the opposition space against AAP and the Congress.
static.wayForward: The durability of the alliance will depend on a mutually acceptable seat-sharing formula, the ability of both parties to transfer votes at the booth level, and whether they can neutralise the farm-law legacy that caused the original split.
prelimsPointers: Punjab Legislative Assembly has 117 seats; the state sends 13 members to the Lok Sabha.
The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded in 1920 and the BJP in 1980.
The anti-defection law is contained in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, inserted in 1985.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how pre-poll alliances alter electoral competition in India, and assess whether they strengthen or weaken programmatic politics and internal party democracy.

static.topic: Punjab's agrarian economy, MSP and farmer movements
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture, MSP and Food Security; role of pressure groups
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price is a price assurance announced by the government on the recommendations of the CACP for 22 mandated crops; it is not a statutory right. Food security is backed by the National Food Security Act, 2013, and the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution.
static.background: The Green Revolution of the 1960s made India food-sufficient and turned Punjab into the country's wheat-paddy granary. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations, PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 a year as income support, and the three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021 after a sustained farmer agitation in which the SAD broke with the NDA.
static.geography: Punjab's wheat-paddy cycle is tied to canal and tubewell irrigation, with falling water tables and stubble burning as recurring consequences.
static.socioEconomic: Farmer unions are among the most organised pressure groups in the state, and their opposition to the BJP-SAD alliance signals that agrarian grievances remain electorally salient.
static.whyInNews: Farmer leaders have described the BJP-SAD alliance as 'highly dangerous' for Punjab, reviving the agrarian question in the run-up to the Assembly polls.
static.wayForward: Crop diversification away from paddy, investment in groundwater recharge and a credible roadmap on procurement and MSP demands would address both farm distress and the political volatility it generates.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement is concentrated in wheat and paddy.
The NFSA, 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
The three farm laws passed in 2020 were repealed in 2021.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how farmer movements have reshaped electoral alliances in Punjab, and evaluate the scope for reforming MSP and procurement without hurting farmer incomes.

static.topic: Regional parties and Indian federalism
static.syllabusNode: Federalism — Regional parties, centre-state relations and party systems
static.whatIsIt: Regional parties are state-level formations that draw their support from a specific linguistic, cultural or territorial constituency and often act as pivotal partners in national coalitions.
static.background: The rise of regional parties from the late 1960s transformed India from a dominant-party system into a coalition era, in which state-level parties became indispensable to government formation at the Centre. The SAD is one of the oldest such parties, and its alliance choices have historically been read as signals about centre-state bargaining.
static.geography: Punjab shares borders with Pakistan and with Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Chandigarh and Rajasthan, giving its politics a distinct border-state sensitivity.
static.socioEconomic: Regional parties typically articulate state-specific economic grievances — in Punjab's case, agrarian distress, industrial stagnation and concerns over fiscal devolution.
static.whyInNews: The SAD-BJP reunion is being read as a test of how regional parties balance state-level identity with national alliance obligations.
static.wayForward: A stable federal bargain requires that regional parties' state-specific concerns be addressed through institutional channels such as the Inter-State Council and Finance Commission transfers, rather than only through electoral arithmetic.
prelimsPointers: The Election Commission recognises parties as national or state parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.
The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body set up under Article 263.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the role of regional parties in India's federal polity and examine whether alliance politics strengthens or dilutes their state-specific agenda.

prelims: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the BJP have announced a pre-poll alliance for the Punjab Assembly elections, after the SAD had left the NDA in 2020 over the farm laws.
Farmer leaders have opposed the alliance, calling it 'highly dangerous' for Punjab; BJP leader Kewal Dhillon has defended it as a step for the state's prosperity.
Punjab has a 117-member Legislative Assembly and 13 Lok Sabha seats.
The SAD was founded in 1920 and the BJP in 1980; the anti-defection law is in the Tenth Schedule (1985).
stories.mainsQuestion: Pre-poll alliances are often described as instruments of opposition consolidation. Using the recent BJP-SAD reunion in Punjab, examine how such alliances reshape electoral competition and what constraints — ideological, agrarian and organisational — determine their durability.

stories.headline: EPG report row tests India's Nepal reset amid China's rise
stories.summary: A fresh row has erupted over the India-Nepal Eminent Persons' Group (EPG) report after Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri described it as "not relevant", prompting former EPG members to insist the document was "highly positive" for bilateral ties. The EPG, constituted in 2016 with four members from each side, submitted its report in 2018, but it was never made public or acted upon by either government. The exchange comes as Delhi attempts a broader reset with Kathmandu spanning connectivity, power trade and people-to-people contacts, while long-standing grievances over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and the Kalapani boundary remain unresolved. Commentators warn that the reset will ultimately be tested by China's expanding economic and diplomatic footprint in Nepal.
stories.whyItMatters: India-Nepal ties sit at the core of GS-II neighbourhood diplomacy, and the EPG episode shows how unresolved structural issues — the 1950 Treaty, the boundary and water-sharing — shape India's standing vis-à-vis China in South Asia.

perspectives.take: Reports the former EPG members' rebuttal, framing the report as constructive and attributing its shelving to political inaction rather than to any deficiency in its content.
Editorial line is self-critical and pro-engagement: India must listen to Nepal's grievances instead of presenting assistance as one-way generosity.
Frames the reset primarily as a strategic contest with China, foregrounding geopolitics over the bilateral grievance-redress agenda.

static.topic: India-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship, 1950
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: A bilateral treaty signed on 31 July 1950 that provides for perpetual peace and friendship, reciprocal treatment of citizens in each other's territory, free movement of people across the open border, national treatment for business and industry, and consultation on foreign policy matters of mutual concern.
static.background: Signed between the governments of India and Nepal, the treaty has been the anchor of the relationship, supplemented over time by periodically renewed trade and transit arrangements, the 1996 Mahakali Treaty on the Pancheshwar project, and defence and security cooperation. Nepal has sought its revision since the 1990s, formally raising the demand in 2001 and again through the Eminent Persons' Group process constituted in 2016.
static.geography: Nepal is a landlocked Himalayan state between India and China, sharing an open border of over 1,700 km with India across Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim.
static.socioEconomic: The open border sustains labour migration, remittances, kinship and cultural ties, and cross-border trade; India is Nepal's largest trading partner and a major source of investment, while the arrangement also raises concerns over undocumented movement and security.
static.whyInNews: The Foreign Secretary's description of the EPG report as "not relevant" and the former members' rebuttal have revived debate on whether the 1950 Treaty framework needs structured revision.
static.wayForward: Pursue a time-bound, structured review through existing bilateral mechanisms, ensuring that any revision safeguards the open-border benefits that underpin livelihoods on both sides.
prelimsPointers: The India-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship was signed on 31 July 1950.
It provides for reciprocal treatment of citizens and consultation on foreign policy matters affecting either country.
Nepal and India share an open border with no visa requirement for citizens of either country.
static.mainsAngle: Should the 1950 Treaty be revised? Examine the tension between Nepal's sovereignty concerns and India's strategic and security interests.

static.topic: Kalapani–Lipulekh–Limpiyadhura Boundary Dispute
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood; boundary disputes
static.whatIsIt: A territorial dispute over roughly 370 sq km at the India-Nepal-China tri-junction, arising from differing interpretations of the source of the Kali river as fixed by the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli.
static.background: The Treaty of Sugauli (1816), which ended the Anglo-Nepal War, fixed the Kali river as Nepal's western boundary. Nepal argues the river originates at Limpiyadhura, while India holds that it rises near Kalapani, where Indian forces have maintained a post since the 1962 conflict. In 2020, India inaugurated a road to Lipulekh on the Kailash Mansarovar route, and Nepal responded by issuing a revised political map incorporating Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura.
static.geography: Located near Pithoragarh district in Uttarakhand, the area is strategically significant as a tri-junction and as the gateway for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route.
static.socioEconomic: The dispute affects border trade, pilgrimage traffic and local communities, and has become a potent symbol in Nepali domestic politics.
static.whyInNews: Along with the EPG report controversy, the unresolved boundary question remains a core irritant in the current phase of India-Nepal engagement.
static.wayForward: Resolve the dispute through the bilateral boundary consultation mechanism, avoiding unilateral cartographic or infrastructure moves that harden positions.
prelimsPointers: The Treaty of Sugauli (1816) fixed the Kali river as Nepal's western boundary.
Nepal's revised political map of 2020 claims about 370 sq km covering Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura.
Lipulekh is a tri-junction pass also used for the Kailash Mansarovar yatra.
static.mainsAngle: Boundary disputes with neighbours test India's neighbourhood diplomacy — discuss with reference to the Kalapani issue.

static.topic: China's Footprint in Nepal and India's Neighbourhood Reset
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood; India and major powers
static.whatIsIt: Nepal's effort to balance its relations between India and China, reflected in Belt and Road cooperation, Chinese-funded infrastructure and connectivity projects, and expanded diplomatic engagement.
static.background: Nepal joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2017 and signed a transit trade agreement with China in 2016 giving it access to Chinese ports, reducing its dependence on Indian transit routes. Chinese contractors have built major infrastructure in Nepal, including the Pokhara regional international airport. India has countered with power trade arrangements, petroleum pipeline and railway connectivity projects, and high-level political engagement.
static.geography: Nepal's landlocked position between India and China, with Himalayan passes such as Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani, makes transit access a central strategic lever.
static.socioEconomic: Chinese lending has raised debt-sustainability questions in Nepal, while India remains its largest trade and investment partner and the principal source of remittances and fuel supply.
static.whyInNews: Analysts frame India's Nepal reset as a test of whether Delhi can retain influence through delivery rather than through pressure.
static.wayForward: Prioritise visible delivery on connectivity, power trade and people-centric projects, and institutionalise regular high-level political and bureaucratic dialogue to rebuild trust.
prelimsPointers: Nepal joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2017.
India is Nepal's largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
The 2016 Nepal-China transit agreement gave Nepal access to Chinese sea ports.
static.mainsAngle: How should India counter China's growing influence in Nepal without appearing coercive? Discuss with reference to India's neighbourhood policy.

prelims: The India-Nepal Eminent Persons' Group was constituted in 2016 with four members from each side and submitted its report in 2018; it has not been made public.
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri described the EPG report as "not relevant", drawing a public rebuttal from former EPG members.
India and Nepal share an open border of over 1,700 km, and India is Nepal's largest trading partner.
The 1816 Treaty of Sugauli fixed the Kali river as Nepal's western boundary, the basis of the Kalapani dispute.
stories.mainsQuestion: India's Nepal policy has oscillated between generosity and grievance-management. Examine the structural irritants in India-Nepal relations and suggest a framework for a durable reset that also addresses China's growing footprint in Nepal.

stories.headline: Iran war drives India, China to record Russian oil imports in 2026
stories.summary: India and China are on course to import record volumes of Russian crude in 2026, with combined purchases reported at roughly 3.4 million barrels a day. The surge is attributed to the Iran war disrupting Middle Eastern supply and to an easing of US sanctions waivers that had earlier constrained such purchases. Analysts across the reports expect the trend to peak, with imports easing in 2027 as Gulf supplies recover and Russian crude loses its price advantage over competing grades. In a related market signal, oil prices touched three-month lows as rising global supply offset the risk premium generated by threats to the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.whyItMatters: The story ties together energy security, sanctions politics and India's external-sector stability — recurring UPSC themes linking geopolitics in West Asia and Europe to India's import bill, inflation and current account. It also illustrates how strategic autonomy plays out in practice when India balances discounted supply against Western sanctions pressure.

perspectives.take: Frames the surge as war-driven supply substitution and foregrounds the 2027 reversal, when recovering Gulf supply and a narrowing Russian discount erode the incentive.
Wire-style, data-led framing that leads on 'demand peaking' — record 2026 volumes but a plateau ahead rather than open-ended growth.
Quantifies the story, putting combined India-China Russian crude sales at 3.4 million barrels a day.
Market-trader lens: treats China and India as the demand engine behind Russian export volumes, with peak demand looming.
Shifts focus to price — oil at three-month lows as rising supply outweighs Hormuz risk; a commodity-market rather than geopolitical frame.

static.topic: India's Energy Security and Crude Oil Import Dependence
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Infrastructure: Energy; also GS-III Security (energy security)
static.whatIsIt: India meets the bulk of its crude requirement through imports, sourced from a diversified basket of West Asian, African, Russian and Americas suppliers; refiners choose grades on price, freight and refining economics.
static.background: India's import dependence rose steadily after domestic production plateaued, with the Indian Basket serving as the reference price for crude. Strategic Petroleum Reserves were built at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur following the oil price spike of the mid-2000s. After 2022, discounted Russian Urals crude became a major component of India's import basket, and public-sector refiners expanded both term and spot purchases.
static.geography: Import routes run through the Strait of Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb and the Malacca Strait; refining capacity is concentrated in Gujarat, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.
static.socioEconomic: Pump prices feed retail inflation and the current account deficit; cheaper crude creates fiscal space for subsidies and buffers households against fuel inflation.
static.whyInNews: India and China are reported to be heading for record Russian crude imports in 2026 as the Iran war disrupts Middle Eastern supply.
static.wayForward: Diversify sourcing, expand strategic reserves, add refining and petrochemical capacity, and scale biofuels, EVs and renewables to blunt import shocks.
prelimsPointers: India is among the world's largest crude oil importers and consumers, with import dependence above 80%.
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how supply-side geopolitics and sanctions shape India's crude sourcing, and what this implies for energy security and macroeconomic stability.

static.topic: India–Russia Strategic Partnership
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations (major powers)
static.whatIsIt: A long-standing 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership' spanning defence hardware, nuclear and space cooperation, energy trade and multilateral coordination.
static.background: Rooted in the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation. Post-1991, ties continued through defence platforms such as the Su-30MKI, T-90, S-400, BrahMos and AK-203 rifles, nuclear reactors at Kudankulam, and connectivity projects including the INSTC and the Vladivostok-Chennai maritime corridor. After 2022, discounted Russian crude became the dominant component of bilateral trade, creating a large trade imbalance in Russia's favour.
static.geography: The INSTC links India to Russia via Iran and the Caspian Sea; the Eastern Maritime Corridor links Chennai and Vladivostok.
static.socioEconomic: Bilateral trade is heavily skewed toward energy imports; rupee-rouble settlement and payment-channel constraints affect the flow of goods.
static.whyInNews: Record Russian crude purchases by India and China in 2026 underline the resilience of energy ties despite Western sanctions.
static.wayForward: Rebalance the trade basket through Indian exports, resolve payment and shipping constraints, and deepen defence co-production and technology transfer.
prelimsPointers: India and the Soviet Union signed the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in 1971.
BrahMos is an India-Russia joint venture, and the S-400 is a Russian-origin air defence system.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how sanctions on Russia test India's strategic autonomy and the durability of the India-Russia partnership.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz and West Asian Energy Chokepoints
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Oceanography and Resources; also GS-II International Relations (West Asia)
static.whatIsIt: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, through which a large share of the world's seaborne crude and LNG moves.
static.background: It has been a flashpoint in successive Gulf conflicts, including the Iran-Iraq war and later tanker incidents, and Iran has repeatedly threatened closure in response to sanctions. Alternative pipelines such as Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline and the UAE's Fujairah line offer only partial bypass capacity.
static.geography: Bounded by Iran to the north and Oman and the UAE to the south; it opens into the Gulf of Oman and thence the Arabian Sea. Other major chokepoints include Bab-el-Mandeb, Suez and Malacca.
static.socioEconomic: Any disruption raises freight and insurance costs, feeding into global crude prices and, for India, into the import bill and inflation.
static.whyInNews: Reports of a Hormuz threat coincided with oil touching three-month lows as rising supply offset the risk premium.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing, maintain strategic reserves, and strengthen naval presence and maritime domain awareness in the Indian Ocean Region.
prelimsPointers: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption is transported through the Strait of Hormuz.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how chokepoint vulnerabilities in West Asia affect India's energy security and what mitigation options are available.

prelims: India and China are reported to be heading for record Russian crude imports in 2026, with combined volumes around 3.4 million barrels a day.
Russia's Urals is its flagship export crude grade; discounted pricing relative to Brent has driven Asian purchases since 2022.
The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, carries roughly a fifth of global oil consumption.
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
stories.mainsQuestion: Examine how geopolitical disruptions in West Asia and the global sanctions architecture shape India's crude oil sourcing strategy. Discuss the implications for India's energy security and external sector stability.

static.whatIsIt: ISRO (1969) runs India's space programme for communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC) and exploration, under the Department of Space. IN-SPACe (2020) and NSIL promote private participation.
static.background: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023. Mangalyaan (2013) reached Mars orbit on its first attempt. Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission.
static.socioEconomic: Space applications support communications, weather forecasting, disaster management, agriculture and governance; private participation through IN-SPACe and NSIL is expanding the space economy.

static.topic: Space-based military surveillance and ISR

static.whatIsIt: Space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) uses satellites to monitor military movements, ports, bases and critical infrastructure. Many satellites are dual-use, serving civilian remote sensing and military reconnaissance.
static.background: Military space surveillance developed during the Cold War. India operates remote-sensing and radar-imaging satellites for strategic and civilian needs. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) prohibits weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not ban military reconnaissance satellites.

static.socioEconomic: Ports and refineries are critical economic infrastructure; surveillance of them has both security and economic implications.
static.whyInNews: Reports claim Chinese satellites focused on Gujarat's coast during Operation Sindoor, raising concerns about foreign ISR over Indian strategic assets.
static.wayForward: India needs enhanced space situational awareness, counter-surveillance capabilities, and a clearer doctrine for space security.
prelimsPointers: The Outer Space Treaty (1967) bans WMD in orbit but does not ban military reconnaissance satellites.
UN COPUOS is the main UN body for space law.

stories.headline: Thiruparankundram Deepam lit as courts spar over compliance with SC order
stories.summary: The Karthigai Deepam was lit at its customary spot on the Thiruparankundram hill near Madurai even as litigation over the ritual continued in the courts. The Supreme Court had permitted the lighting of the deepathoon as a one-time measure, and the Madras High Court, hearing the fallout, restrained protests against that order while asking the Tamil Nadu government to reconsider the prohibitory orders imposed in Madurai. The High Court clarified that judicial orders may be criticised, even through strong remarks, but no one may call for their non-compliance, and observed that pendency of a review is no ground for non-compliance with a Supreme Court order. The episode has sharpened the contest between judicially regulated ritual arrangements, the state's law-and-order powers and competing claims over temple custom.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the constitutional duty of compliance with Supreme Court orders (Articles 141 and 144), the High Court's supervisory role, and the state's public-order powers — recurring GS-II themes of judicial review, federalism and religious freedom.

perspectives.take: Frames the outcome narrowly as a one-time permission to light the deepathoon, foregrounding the apex court's calibrated, interim approach to a sensitive ritual dispute.
Regional, ground-level account that the lamp was lit at the customary spot notwithstanding the court orders, focusing on events on the hill rather than the legal reasoning.

static.topic: Compliance with Supreme Court orders and the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) supervise subordinate courts and the executive within their territory. Judicial review is the power to test executive and legislative action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s; Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Madras High Court restrained protests against the Supreme Court's order on the Thiruparankundram deepam and held that pendency of a review is no ground for non-compliance.
static.wayForward: Strengthen institutional mechanisms for compliance reporting and use contempt sparingly, while protecting reasoned criticism of judgments and enforcing the binding character of apex court orders.
prelimsPointers: Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India.

static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the binding nature of Supreme Court orders (Articles 141 and 144) interacts with the right to protest and dissent in a constitutional democracy.

static.topic: Law and order, prohibitory orders and state executive power
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: public order and police are State List subjects, so state governments impose prohibitory orders to maintain peace, subject to judicial review.
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined the Centre-State balance; the Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative; law and order remains a state responsibility under the Seventh Schedule.
static.geography: Thiruparankundram is a hillock near Madurai, Tamil Nadu, home to a rock-cut Murugan temple, one of the six Arupadai Veedu abodes of Lord Murugan.
static.socioEconomic: Temple festivals are major local cultural and economic events; restrictions affect pilgrim footfall, local livelihoods and communal harmony in the district.
static.whyInNews: The Madras High Court asked the Tamil Nadu government to reconsider the prohibitory orders imposed in Madurai during the deepam dispute.
static.wayForward: Balance public order with religious freedom through consultative, time-bound local administration and transparent, reviewable criteria for imposing restrictions.
prelimsPointers: 'Public order' and 'police' are State List entries, while 'criminal law' and 'criminal procedure' fall in the Concurrent List.
The Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory body for inter-state coordination and dispute resolution.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how state law-and-order powers interact with judicially recognised religious practices, and whether the federal balance is respected in such disputes.

static.topic: Religious freedom, temple customs and state regulation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Articles 25–26)
static.whatIsIt: Articles 25–26 guarantee freedom of conscience, the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, and the rights of religious denominations, subject to public order, morality and health; the state may regulate the secular aspects of religion.
static.background: Temple administration in Tamil Nadu is regulated under the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959; courts have applied the 'essential religious practices' test since the Shirur Mutt case (1954) to decide what is constitutionally protected.
static.socioEconomic: Customary ritual rights often carry prestige, patronage and local economic stakes, which makes disputes over them socially volatile.
static.whyInNews: The dispute over who lights the deepam at Thiruparankundram raises questions of custom, denominational rights and state regulation of temple rituals.
static.wayForward: Prefer mediated, locally negotiated settlements recorded in writing, with courts intervening only to protect constitutional rights and maintain public order.
prelimsPointers: Article 25 rights are available to all persons, including non-citizens, while Article 26 rights belong to religious denominations.
Article 25(2)(a) permits the state to regulate or restrict secular activities associated with religious practice.
static.mainsAngle: To what extent can the state regulate temple customs and rituals? Discuss with reference to Articles 25–26 and the essential religious practices doctrine.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu to sign 70 investment deals worth over ₹50,000 crore
stories.summary: Tamil Nadu is set to announce around 70 investment deals valued at over ₹50,000 crore (about $5.38 billion) at an investor conclave in Chennai. The agreements span manufacturing, clean energy, electronics and textiles, and the event will also feature foundation-stone layings and inaugurations of projects. The rupee figure comes from domestic business reporting, while the dollar estimate was reported by a wire service citing people familiar with the plans. Together the two accounts indicate a state-level push to convert announced investor interest into signed commitments and ground-level capacity. The deals are announcements or memoranda of intent, and their eventual conversion into actual investment remains the key variable to watch.
stories.whyItMatters: State-level investor conclaves are the practical face of competitive federalism and of India's manufacturing and clean-energy ambitions, making them relevant to questions on industrial policy, FDI and Centre-State economic relations. The gap between MoUs signed and investment actually grounded is a standard evaluation angle in GS-II and GS-III answers.

static.topic: Competitive federalism and State investment conclaves
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: State-hosted investor conclaves and the memoranda of understanding signed there are an instrument of competitive federalism: states market themselves directly to domestic and foreign investors within the division of powers set by the Seventh Schedule.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) examined the Centre-State balance. Post-1991 liberalisation moved much industrial and investment facilitation to the states, and NITI Aayog has since promoted competitive federalism through state ranking indices. Tamil Nadu has used successive editions of its own investor meet as a recurring platform for signing MoUs across sectors.
static.geography: Tamil Nadu is a southern peninsular state with a long coastline and the Chennai industrial belt, which is a major hub for automobiles, auto components and electronics assembly; the state is also among India's leading wind-energy producers.
static.socioEconomic: Announced MoUs are intentions, not realised capital. Actual outcomes depend on land availability, power and logistics costs, single-window clearances, skilled labour supply and the conversion rate from signed agreement to grounded project.
static.whyInNews: Tamil Nadu is announcing about 70 investment deals worth over ₹50,000 crore at a Chennai investor conclave covering manufacturing, clean energy, electronics and textiles.
static.wayForward: Publish MoU-to-ground conversion data, strengthen single-window clearance and land banks, and align state skilling missions with the sectors being signed up so that announcements translate into jobs and output.
prelimsPointers: Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) dealt with Centre-State relations.
The Seventh Schedule divides powers into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, with residuary powers with the Union (Article 248).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for inter-state disputes and coordination.
static.mainsAngle: State investment conclaves are often cited as proof of competitive federalism — assess whether the MoU model delivers durable investment or mostly generates publicity.

static.topic: Make in India, FDI policy and manufacturing competitiveness
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Industrial Policy, Investment & Growth
static.whatIsIt: Make in India, launched on 25 September 2014, seeks to make India a global manufacturing and design hub. It works alongside a liberalised FDI regime, where most sectors allow foreign investment under the automatic route, and Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes that reward incremental output.
static.background: The 1991 reforms dismantled industrial licensing and opened the economy; the New Industrial Policy of 1991 was followed by the National Manufacturing Policy (2011) and then Make in India (2014). Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and the PLI schemes extended support to targeted sectors, and the National Logistics Policy (2022) addressed logistics costs.
static.socioEconomic: Manufacturing has hovered around the mid-teens as a share of gross value added, well short of the 25% of GDP aspiration set out in the National Manufacturing Policy. Investment announcements in electronics, textiles and clean energy are read as a test of whether that share can rise.
static.whyInNews: The Tamil Nadu deals cover manufacturing, electronics and textiles — the same sectors that anchor Make in India and PLI-driven capacity creation.
static.wayForward: Focus on reducing compliance and logistics costs, deepening supplier ecosystems for components rather than only assembly, and building vocational pipelines so capital investment is matched by employable labour.
prelimsPointers: Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014.
FDI is prohibited in sectors such as lottery, gambling and betting, chit funds, real estate business or farm houses, tobacco manufacturing, and atomic energy.
The National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 set a target of raising manufacturing to 25% of GDP.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why manufacturing's share of GDP has stagnated despite successive industrial policies, and evaluate whether state-level investment drives can correct this.

static.topic: Clean energy manufacturing and India's non-fossil capacity target
static.syllabusNode: Economy / Environment — Energy Transition & Green Manufacturing
static.whatIsIt: India has committed to installing 500 GW of non-fossil fuel electricity generation capacity by 2030, announced as part of the Panchamrit pledges at COP26 in Glasgow (2021). Domestic manufacturing of solar modules, cells and battery storage is being supported through PLI schemes to reduce import dependence.
static.background: The National Solar Mission dates to 2010. India's updated Nationally Determined Contribution targets about 50% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, alongside a net-zero-by-2070 pledge. Solar PV module and advanced chemistry cell battery PLI schemes were introduced to build a domestic supply chain.
static.geography: Tamil Nadu has strong wind resources, particularly in the southern districts, and growing solar capacity, making it a natural host for clean-energy investment commitments.
static.socioEconomic: Green manufacturing promises jobs and lower emissions but faces challenges of land, transmission evacuation infrastructure and the cost competitiveness of domestic components against imports.
static.whyInNews: Clean energy is among the four sectors named in Tamil Nadu's new investment deal package.
static.wayForward: Pair generation capacity targets with grid and storage investment, and ensure domestic manufacturing incentives build component depth rather than only final assembly.
prelimsPointers: The Panchamrit pledges were announced by India at COP26, Glasgow in 2021.
India's updated NDC targets about 50% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources by 2030.
India has pledged net-zero emissions by 2070.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India can reconcile its 500 GW non-fossil capacity target with the goal of building a self-reliant domestic clean-energy manufacturing base.

prelims: Tamil Nadu is set to announce around 70 investment deals worth over ₹50,000 crore, reported as about $5.38 billion by Reuters.
The deals cover manufacturing, clean energy, electronics and textiles, and the Chennai conclave also includes foundation-stone layings and project inaugurations.
Investment MoUs are statements of intent; they are not the same as realised FDI or grounded capacity.
stories.mainsQuestion: State-level investor conclaves have become a prominent instrument of competitive federalism in India. Examine the extent to which such MoU-driven investment announcements translate into grounded industrial capacity, and suggest measures to improve conversion.

stories.headline: US jury convicts Huawei of trade secret theft, bank fraud; racketeering acquittal
stories.summary: A US federal jury has convicted Chinese technology major Huawei of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud, while acquitting the company of racketeering. The prosecution alleged that the firm conspired to misappropriate trade secrets from a US company and breached US sanctions by doing business in countries such as Iran and North Korea, then made false statements to banks and US government officials to conceal the conduct. The verdict follows a lengthy trial that grew out of a years-long US investigation and a 2019 indictment against the company and its chief financial officer. Huawei has consistently denied wrongdoing, and Beijing has in the past dismissed such US legal actions as politically motivated. The outcome is likely to further harden the already contested terrain of US-China trade and technology relations.
stories.whyItMatters: The verdict shows how trade secrets, sanctions and national security have fused into economic statecraft — a recurring theme in US-China rivalry questions. It also raises issues of extraterritorial jurisdiction and supply-chain trust relevant to India's telecom and technology policy.

perspectives.take: Straight wire-style account centred on the guilty finding, also foregrounding the alleged sanctions violations involving Iran and North Korea and false statements to US officials and banks.
