static.topic: US–China Strategic and Technological Rivalry
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations and Global Groupings (US–China)
static.whatIsIt: Structural competition between the world's two largest economies spanning trade, technology standards, military posture and competing models of global governance.
static.background: Trade friction escalated from 2018 with US tariffs justified under Section 301 of the Trade Act, 1974. Huawei was added to the US Commerce Department's Entity List in May 2019, after the December 2018 arrest of its CFO in Canada and a 2019 US indictment against the firm. Tensions widened with export controls on advanced semiconductors from 2022 and US legislation such as the CHIPS and Science Act (2022) aimed at reshoring chip manufacturing capacity.
static.geography: Principal theatres of friction are East Asia and the South China Sea, with supply-chain chokepoints in Taiwan and the wider Indo-Pacific.
static.socioEconomic: The two economies remain deeply interdependent; decoupling raises costs, distorts technology access and feeds global inflationary pressure, while pushing 'de-risking' and friend-shoring strategies.
static.whyInNews: A US federal jury convicted Huawei of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, deepening the technology-and-security dimension of the rivalry.
static.wayForward: India should hedge through diversified supply chains, active engagement in plurilateral technology arrangements and a clear position on rules for export controls and data security.
prelimsPointers: Huawei was placed on the US Commerce Department's Entity List in 2019.
Section 301 of the US Trade Act, 1974 is a key legal basis for US tariff actions against China.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the securitisation of trade and technology is reshaping the rules-based trading order and what strategic options it leaves for India.

static.topic: Economic Sanctions, Extraterritoriality and Export Controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Economic Diplomacy; Sanctions and Coercive Economic Measures
static.whatIsIt: Use of sanctions, asset freezes, trade restrictions and export controls by states — chiefly the US — to pursue foreign policy and national security objectives, often reaching entities outside their territory.
static.background: US sanctions are largely administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in the Treasury. Sanctions on Iran intensified after the US exited the JCPOA (2015 nuclear deal) in 2018, with secondary sanctions penalising third-country entities. India has had to balance such measures against its energy and connectivity interests, including the Chabahar port project, and has used instruments such as rupee-based settlement and, historically, engagement with European mechanisms like INSTEX.
static.geography: Sanctions touch global dollar-clearing networks, oil shipping routes, and specific corridors such as Chabahar in Iran.
static.socioEconomic: Secondary sanctions raise compliance costs, insurance and shipping premiums, and can disrupt energy security and trade finance for third countries, including India.
static.whyInNews: The Huawei case involved allegations of business in sanctions-hit jurisdictions such as Iran and North Korea and of false statements to banks — a textbook illustration of extraterritorial enforcement.
static.wayForward: India's approach has been to seek targeted waivers, diversify payment and settlement channels, and push for rules-based multilateral discipline on unilateral coercive measures.
prelimsPointers: GATT Article XXI provides a national-security exception invoked by members to justify trade restrictions.
US sanctions on Iran are principally administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) under the US Treasury.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the challenge unilateral sanctions and extraterritorial enforcement pose to the multilateral trading system and to India's strategic autonomy.

static.topic: India's Telecom Security and Trusted Supply Chains
static.syllabusNode: Security — Cyber and Telecom Security; Science & Technology — Emerging Technologies
static.whatIsIt: A regime to ensure telecom networks are built only with equipment from 'trusted sources', linking national security to procurement in the telecom sector.
static.background: The National Security Directive on Telecommunication Sector (NSDTS) was approved in December 2020 and took effect from June 2021, creating a National Security Committee on telecom to designate trusted sources and trusted products. Huawei and ZTE were kept out of India's 5G trials announced in 2021. India's 5G spectrum auction was held in 2022 and 5G services were launched in October 2022.
static.socioEconomic: Vendor concentration and import dependence in telecom equipment affect operator costs, network resilience and the pace of digital inclusion.
static.whyInNews: The Huawei verdict reinforces global scrutiny of vendor trustworthiness, a concern already embedded in India's telecom procurement policy.
static.wayForward: Diversify the vendor base, invest in indigenous R&D and standards capability, and strengthen telecom cybersecurity auditing and certification.
prelimsPointers: India's 5G spectrum auction was held in 2022, with 5G services launched in October 2022.
The National Security Directive on Telecommunication Sector (2020) established a trusted-source regime effective from June 2021.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how national-security considerations are reshaping India's telecom equipment procurement and what it means for digital sovereignty and cost of connectivity.

prelims: A US federal jury convicted Huawei of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud, but acquitted it of racketeering.
The case also involved allegations of business in countries under US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and of false statements to US banks and government officials.
Huawei had been placed on the US Commerce Department's Entity List in 2019, following the 2018 arrest of its chief financial officer in Canada.
stories.mainsQuestion: The conviction of a major Chinese technology firm by a US court shows how trade secrets, sanctions and national security have become entangled in economic statecraft. Examine the implications of this trend for the multilateral trading system and for India's technology and supply-chain policy.

stories.headline: Eisenkot clinches first coalition deal in bid to form Israeli government
stories.summary: Israeli politician Eisenkot has secured his first coalition agreement in his attempt to put together a governing majority, according to reports. His party, referred to in the reports as Yashar, said he met Avigdor Lieberman, head of the Israel Our Home (Yisrael Beiteinu) party, and that the two sides reached a deal afterwards. The agreement is the first building block in a wider coalition jigsaw that would still need the backing of a majority in the Knesset. The development signals a possible realignment of Israeli politics around a figure drawn from the security establishment, with Lieberman's party — historically strong on security and on the secular-right — as an early partner. Talks with other parties are expected to continue before any government can be sworn in.
stories.whyItMatters: Israel's coalition arithmetic shapes West Asia's security trajectory, and any change of government in Jerusalem directly affects India's defence, technology and connectivity engagements with the region. Coalition formation is a standard UPSC theme for comparative politics and for GS-II questions on the politics of developed and developing countries.

static.topic: Israel's coalition politics and government formation
static.syllabusNode: Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: Israel has a unicameral legislature, the Knesset, elected through a nationwide proportional representation system with a single country-wide constituency. Because no single party normally wins a majority, the President consults parties and tasks a member with assembling a coalition that can command the confidence of the House.
static.background: Israel's proportional system and low electoral threshold have historically produced fragmented parliaments, frequent early elections and multi-party coalitions, including national unity and rotational arrangements. Eisenkot, a former IDF Chief of Staff who entered politics in recent years, is now attempting to build such a coalition, beginning with Avigdor Lieberman's Israel Our Home (Yisrael Beiteinu) party.
static.geography: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean, bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt, with the West Bank and Gaza Strip adjoining it — a compact, strategically located state with limited strategic depth.
static.socioEconomic: Coalition negotiations in Israel typically turn on the budget, cost of living, military conscription of ultra-Orthodox communities, religion–state issues and settlement policy, each of which is a bargaining chip for smaller parties.
static.whyInNews: Eisenkot has clinched his first coalition agreement, with Lieberman's Israel Our Home party, in his bid to form a government.
static.wayForward: The coalition must still reach a majority in the 120-member Knesset and survive a confidence vote; further agreements with additional parties will determine whether a stable government emerges or the country heads towards another election.
prelimsPointers: The Knesset has 120 members; a government needs the support of at least 61 members.
Israel elects the Knesset from a single nationwide constituency under proportional representation.
static.mainsAngle: Compare coalition government formation in Israel with India's parliamentary system, and examine how fragmented legislatures affect policy stability and foreign-policy continuity.

static.topic: India–Israel relations
static.syllabusNode: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India and Israel maintain a multi-dimensional relationship spanning defence procurement, agriculture and water technology, counter-terrorism cooperation, cyber and innovation, and increasingly connectivity and trade groupings.
static.background: India established full diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992, and defence and agricultural cooperation expanded substantially thereafter. India has also pursued de-hyphenated ties with Israel and Palestine, and joined the I2U2 grouping with Israel, the UAE and the United States, alongside the proposed India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor.
static.geography: Israel sits at the junction of the eastern Mediterranean and West Asia, close to the Suez Canal and the Red Sea approaches, giving it significance for trade routes and energy flows that matter to India.
static.socioEconomic: Indian exports of labour, agricultural technology partnerships and defence offsets link the two economies; Israeli technology is used in Indian agriculture, water management and homeland security.
static.whyInNews: A change in Israel's governing coalition could alter the political complexion of a government that India deals with on defence, technology and West Asian connectivity.
static.wayForward: India should continue to insulate its functional cooperation with Israel from coalition churn, while balancing its traditional ties with Palestine and its partnerships with Gulf states.
prelimsPointers: India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992.
I2U2 groups India, Israel, the UAE and the United States.

static.topic: Coalition governments and political stability — comparative perspective
static.syllabusNode: Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; Parliament and State legislatures — structure, functioning and comparison
static.whatIsIt: Coalition government is a system in which two or more parties combine to command a legislative majority, typically under a common minimum programme and a power-sharing arrangement.
static.background: India experienced coalition governments at the Union level from the late 1980s onwards, which produced the era of common minimum programmes and coordination committees. Israel's proportional system makes coalitions the norm rather than the exception, with smaller parties extracting policy concessions.
static.socioEconomic: Coalitions often trade long-term policy coherence for immediate majority-building, affecting budget discipline, reform sequencing and the credibility of commitments to external partners.
static.whyInNews: Eisenkot's first coalition agreement illustrates how fragmented legislatures force negotiated power-sharing before a government can take office.
static.wayForward: Stable coalition management requires written common agendas, institutionalised coordination mechanisms and clear dispute-resolution channels between partners.
prelimsPointers: A government must demonstrate majority support on the floor of the legislature to assume office.
Proportional representation systems generally produce multi-party legislatures more often than first-past-the-post systems.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether proportional representation improves representation at the cost of governmental stability, using Israel and India as comparative cases.

stories.headline: CIA and ODNI suffer cyber breach of unclassified information
stories.summary: Reports on 24 November 2026 said the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence suffered a cybersecurity breach involving unclassified information. The compromised material reportedly included data from CIA's open-source intelligence system, while no classified information was said to be involved. It was not immediately clear exactly what unclassified material was taken, and information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed. The incident comes amid a series of disruptions affecting U.S. national security agencies, technology companies, banks and critical infrastructure.

static.topic: Cyber Security and Critical Information Infrastructure
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security: Cyber Security
static.whatIsIt: Cyber security protects networks, systems and data from unauthorised access, disruption or damage; critical information infrastructure refers to strategic systems whose failure can affect national security.
static.background: India's cyber-security architecture includes CERT-In as the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response, NATGRID for intelligence support, and Integrated Command and Control Centres. The IT Act, 2000 provides the legal framework for cyber offences and incident response.
static.whyInNews: The CIA and ODNI breach shows that even unclassified information held by intelligence agencies can be targeted, raising concerns for critical information infrastructure.
static.wayForward: Strengthen classification and access controls, invest in zero-trust architecture, conduct regular audits, expand CERT-In capacity, and deepen international cyber cooperation.

NATGRID and Integrated Command and Control Centres support India's internal security and cyber-security architecture.

static.topic: Data Governance and Protection of Unclassified Information
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data
static.whatIsIt: Data governance covers rules for collecting, classifying, storing, sharing and protecting data, including personal and official information.
static.background: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing through consent and data-principal rights, and provides for a Data Protection Board and obligations on significant data fiduciaries.
static.socioEconomic: Breaches of official data can affect privacy, public trust and national security, even when the data is unclassified.
static.whyInNews: The reported breach of unclassified US intelligence information underscores the need for robust data classification and protection even for non-classified material.
static.wayForward: Adopt clear data-classification norms, breach-notification protocols, access controls, and privacy-by-design in government systems.
prelimsPointers: The DPDP Act, 2023 provides for consent-based processing and data-principal rights.
It establishes a Data Protection Board and obligations for significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Balance innovation and state surveillance with privacy; discuss how data-governance frameworks can protect both personal and official unclassified data.

The reported breach involved unclassified information, not classified data, according to the accounts.
CIA's open-source intelligence system was reportedly among the affected systems.

stories.mainsQuestion: Cyber breaches of intelligence agencies, even when unclassified information is involved, can have significant national security implications. Discuss the challenges in securing critical information infrastructure and suggest measures to strengthen cyber resilience in India.

stories.headline: AMR Awareness Week turns focus to antibiotic overuse in poultry and livestock
stories.summary: Marking World AMR Awareness Week, Down To Earth ran a three-part series arguing that India's antimicrobial resistance problem cannot be solved inside hospitals alone, because routine antibiotic use in poultry and livestock is a major driver. One article focuses on poultry, showing that better biosecurity, shed hygiene, ventilation and balanced nutrition reduce disease pressure and therefore the need for prophylactic medication. A second looks at livestock, where improved fodder quality and rations lower metabolic stress and disease incidence, cutting reliance on antibiotics including for growth promotion. The third widens the frame, urging policymakers to look beyond clinical settings to farms, feed and the environment. Read together, the series makes a One Health case that farm-level management, not just prescription control, must anchor India's AMR response.
stories.whyItMatters: AMR is a cross-cutting UPSC theme linking public health, animal husbandry, food safety and environmental regulation, and it is a live example of the One Health approach in policy. It also lets aspirants connect agriculture and welfare questions to India's international health commitments.

perspectives.take: Poultry-focused piece: frames farm-level biosecurity, shed hygiene and nutrition as the cheapest route to healthier flocks and lower antibiotic use; awareness-advocacy tone.
Livestock-focused piece: puts fodder quality and ration balancing at the centre, arguing that better nutrition reduces disease and hence antibiotic dependence in dairy and other livestock.
Policy-focused piece: critiques the hospital-centric framing of AMR and pushes a One Health lens covering farms, feed and the environment; developmental-reporting, pro-regulation orientation.

static.topic: Antimicrobial Resistance and the One Health approach
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Health; Environment & Ecology — One Health
static.whatIsIt: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites evolve to survive medicines that once killed them, making infections harder to treat. One Health recognises that human, animal, plant and environmental health are interlinked, so AMR must be tackled across sectors rather than in hospitals alone.
static.background: The WHO Global Action Plan on AMR (2015) asked member states to prepare national action plans on a One Health basis. India responded with its National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance for 2017–2021, covering human health, animal husbandry, fisheries, agriculture and the environment. The ICMR runs an AMR Surveillance and Research Network that tracks resistance patterns in tertiary-care hospitals. The Ministry of Health's 'Red Line' campaign (2016) marked prescription-only antibiotics to discourage self-medication, and Kerala has been widely cited for its antibiotic literacy initiative. WHO's AWaRe classification groups antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve categories to guide stewardship.
static.socioEconomic: Antibiotic use in animals is shaped by price signals, market demand for faster growth and thin awareness among small producers; resistance in animals can spill into humans through the food chain, water and direct contact, raising treatment costs for households.
static.whyInNews: World AMR Awareness Week has spotlighted antibiotic use in poultry and livestock, with Down To Earth arguing that farm-level practices, not just hospital prescribing, must anchor the response.
static.wayForward: Tighten regulation of antibiotics as growth promoters, strengthen veterinary prescription oversight, expand surveillance to animals and the environment, build extension capacity for farmers, and promote vaccination, biosecurity and improved nutrition as substitutes for routine medication.
keyTerms: ICMR AMR Surveillance and Research Network
prelimsPointers: World AMR Awareness Week is observed annually from 18 to 24 November.
WHO's AWaRe classification places antibiotics in Access, Watch and Reserve groups to guide stewardship.
India's National Action Plan on AMR (2017–2021) adopted a One Health approach spanning human, animal and environmental health.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how agricultural antibiotic use complicates India's fight against AMR, and evaluate the adequacy of the One Health framework in Indian policy.

static.topic: Livestock and poultry in India's agricultural economy
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture & Food Security; Animal Husbandry
static.whatIsIt: Livestock and poultry form the allied sector of Indian agriculture, contributing to farm incomes, protein nutrition and rural employment through dairy, meat, eggs and draught power. Productivity depends on feed and fodder, breeding, animal health and market access.
static.background: The Green Revolution of the 1960s made India cereal-sufficient but left allied sectors relatively under-supported. MSP is announced by the government on CACP recommendations for 22 mandated crops, and procurement remains concentrated in wheat and paddy. The National Food Security Act, 2013 backs food security, and PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year as income support to eligible farmer households. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations, and the three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021. Livestock-specific support has come through the National Livestock Mission and the Rashtriya Gokul Mission.
static.geography: Dairy livestock density is high in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab; commercial poultry clusters are concentrated in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu.
static.socioEconomic: Livestock acts as an income buffer against crop failure, especially for small and marginal farmers and landless households, and women's participation is significant in backyard poultry and dairy. Feed costs dominate producer economics, making fodder quality a direct determinant of viability.
static.whyInNews: The AMR Awareness Week series argues that fodder quality, nutrition and management in poultry and livestock can reduce disease and thereby cut routine antibiotic use.
static.wayForward: Invest in fodder and feed quality, expand veterinary and extension services, strengthen animal disease surveillance, and integrate antibiotic-use data from farms into national AMR monitoring.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance announced for 22 mandated crops on CACP recommendations, not a legal right.
NFSA 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year as direct income support to eligible farmer households.
static.mainsAngle: How can India raise livestock and poultry productivity while reducing antimicrobial dependence? Examine the role of feed, fodder and extension policy.

static.topic: Health, welfare architecture and the cost of resistance
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model combines rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the RTE Act (2009) and the NFSA (2013) with DBT-enabled delivery through the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone. Ayushman Bharat (2018) has an insurance arm, PM-JAY, alongside Health and Wellness Centres.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018 with PM-JAY providing health cover and Health and Wellness Centres delivering comprehensive primary care. POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. Articles 15 and 16, along with Indra Sawhney (1992), frame reservation policy. Four labour codes consolidate 29 labour laws.
static.socioEconomic: High out-of-pocket health expenditure remains a major cause of household distress; resistant infections lengthen hospital stays and raise costs, eroding the financial protection that PM-JAY is meant to provide.
static.whyInNews: The AMR Awareness Week series argues that curbing resistance requires action beyond hospitals, implicating farm practices, food systems and regulatory oversight that sit outside conventional health policy.
static.wayForward: Link AMR control to health-financing reform, strengthen primary-care stewardship, regulate over-the-counter and veterinary antibiotic sales, and integrate One Health surveillance into national health programmes.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how antimicrobial resistance threatens the financial-protection objectives of India's health welfare architecture, and suggest reforms.

prelims: World AMR Awareness Week is observed every year from 18 to 24 November.
WHO's AWaRe classification divides antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve groups to guide rational use.
India's National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (2017–2021) adopted a One Health approach covering human, animal, fishery, agriculture and environment sectors.
ICMR's AMR Surveillance and Research Network monitors resistance trends across tertiary-care hospitals in India.
stories.mainsQuestion: Antimicrobial resistance is as much an agricultural problem as a medical one. Examine how antibiotic use in poultry and livestock contributes to AMR in India, and suggest regulatory and farm-level measures to address it.

stories.headline: Kala-azar resurfaces in non-endemic Uttarakhand, testing India's elimination claims
stories.summary: A report from a remote village in Uttarakhand's Pauri region, reachable only by a long downhill footpath from a solar farm, documents kala-azar cases in a state that has never been part of India's traditional endemic belt. The finding sits awkwardly against the country's long-running claim of having brought visceral leishmaniasis close to elimination, a status measured block-wise against a low case threshold. The story frames the detection as a surveillance and ecology question: whether a disease long associated with the Gangetic plains is now appearing in Himalayan foothill settings, and whether elimination declarations rest on data that misses the hardest-to-reach settlements. It also raises the practical issue of access — diagnosis, treatment and follow-up in a village where the road itself gives out.
stories.whyItMatters: Disease elimination claims are a recurring UPSC theme under health policy and social justice; this case tests how elimination is defined, measured and verified, and how health federalism works when a State outside the endemic list reports cases.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a gap between declared elimination and ground-level surveillance, using an environment-and-access lens on a remote Himalayan village where the road ends before the settlement begins.

articles.title: India thought it eliminated kala-azar. The disease now gets reported from a non-endemic state

It ends at a solar farm, narrows into rubble and eventually becomes a stony footpath that winds downhill for about 20 minutes to Chair Talla, a village in Uttarakhand situated at an altitude of 1,100 metres. static.topic: Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis) and India's Elimination Programme
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health, Welfare Schemes and Disease Elimination
static.whatIsIt: Kala-azar, or visceral leishmaniasis, is a parasitic disease caused by Leishmania donovani and transmitted by the bite of the female sandfly Phlebotomus argentipes. It presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, enlarged spleen and liver, and is fatal if untreated. India's elimination programme treats it as a public health problem to be reduced below a defined case threshold at block level, rather than as complete eradication.
static.background: India has run a dedicated kala-azar control effort since the 1990s under the vector-borne disease programme, later folded into the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control. The endemic belt has historically been concentrated in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and eastern Uttar Pradesh, with Bihar accounting for the largest share. Elimination was defined as fewer than one case per 10,000 population at block level, and India has repeatedly revised its target year. Kala-azar is also on the WHO list of neglected tropical diseases, whose roadmap seeks elimination as a public health problem by 2030.
static.geography: Historically endemic: Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and eastern Uttar Pradesh in the Gangetic plains. The news reports cases from a village in Uttarakhand at about 1,100 metres altitude, outside the recognised endemic belt.
static.socioEconomic: Kala-azar is strongly associated with poverty — mud-walled housing, cattle sheds near dwellings that harbour sandflies, and poor access to early diagnosis. Delayed treatment pushes households into catastrophic health expenditure, and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis can act as a persistent human reservoir.
static.whyInNews: A report documents kala-azar from a non-endemic Himalayan state, raising questions about the completeness of elimination surveillance and about whether vector ecology is shifting.
static.wayForward: Strengthen active case-finding and laboratory confirmation in non-endemic and hard-to-reach districts; integrate kala-azar surveillance with the broader vector-borne disease and primary health centre network; maintain indoor residual spraying and sandfly control where cases appear; and publish block-level data transparently so elimination claims can be independently verified.
keyTerms: Elimination as a public health problem
prelimsPointers: Kala-azar is caused by the protozoan Leishmania donovani and spread by the sandfly Phlebotomus argentipes; it is not spread person-to-person by casual contact.
India's elimination benchmark has been fewer than one case per 10,000 population at block level, not zero cases.
Kala-azar features on the WHO neglected tropical disease list, whose roadmap targets elimination as a public health problem by 2030.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why disease elimination in India is better described as a threshold-based public health target than as eradication, and assess the surveillance architecture needed to make such claims credible.

static.topic: Health as a State Subject and Centre-State Coordination in Disease Control
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism and Devolution of Powers
static.whatIsIt: Public health, hospitals and sanitation are State List subjects under the Seventh Schedule, while the Union handles matters such as interstate quarantine, port health and national-level disease programmes. National elimination and surveillance programmes therefore operate through cooperative arrangements between the Union health ministry, State health departments and district administrations.
static.background: The constitutional division of powers places the primary duty for health delivery on States, with the Centre funding and steering national programmes. Commissions such as Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) examined Centre-State balance more broadly. In practice, national health missions, centrally sponsored schemes and shared data platforms have produced a heavily cooperative — and sometimes contested — model of health federalism.
static.socioEconomic: States with weaker fiscal capacity and thin health infrastructure depend disproportionately on central transfers, which shapes how quickly a district can respond to an unexpected outbreak.
static.whyInNews: A disease historically confined to a few endemic States being reported from another State tests how Union and State health machinery share surveillance, funding and response duties.
static.wayForward: Move towards interoperable, district-level disease surveillance data shared across States; use the Inter-State Council and national programme platforms for coordinated outbreak response; and align central funding with the actual burden reported by States rather than with historical endemic lists.
prelimsPointers: Public health and sanitation are State List entries; the Union's role in health is largely through national programmes, standards and interstate quarantine.
The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory body for coordination and dispute resolution between States and the Union.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how health federalism shapes India's capacity to detect and respond to diseases appearing outside their historically endemic regions.

static.topic: Neglected Tropical Diseases and the WHO 2021–2030 Roadmap
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health and International Cooperation
static.whatIsIt: Neglected tropical diseases are a group of communicable diseases, including kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis, leprosy and soil-transmitted helminthiases, that disproportionately affect poor and remote populations. The WHO roadmap for 2021–2030 sets targets for their control, elimination and eradication.
static.background: The earlier WHO roadmap set 2020 targets, several of which were missed; the current roadmap extends timelines to 2030 and emphasises integrated, cross-cutting interventions rather than disease-specific vertical programmes. India is a signatory to these global goals and runs aligned national programmes.
static.geography: NTDs cluster in tropical and subtropical regions with limited health infrastructure; in India they concentrate in the poorest districts of the eastern and central belt.
static.socioEconomic: NTDs reinforce poverty cycles through disability, stigma and lost productivity, and are typically absent from the priorities of both markets and weak public health systems.
static.whyInNews: The reappearance of kala-azar outside its endemic zone illustrates why NTD elimination targets depend on surveillance reaching the last settlement, not just on aggregate case counts.
static.wayForward: Integrate NTD screening into primary health care and existing vector-borne disease platforms; invest in point-of-care diagnostics for remote areas; and link NTD programmes with housing, sanitation and nutrition interventions that address underlying risk factors.
keyTerms: Elimination as a public health problem
prelimsPointers: The WHO NTD roadmap 2021–2030 replaced the earlier 2020 roadmap and sets 2030 targets for control, elimination and eradication.
Kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis and leprosy are among the NTDs targeted by India's national programmes.
static.mainsAngle: Critically examine why neglected tropical disease elimination targets are repeatedly missed, and suggest how India can integrate NTD response into primary health care.

prelims: Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is caused by Leishmania donovani and transmitted by the sandfly Phlebotomus argentipes.
India's elimination benchmark for kala-azar has been fewer than one case per 10,000 population at block level, not zero incidence.
Public health and sanitation are State List subjects under the Seventh Schedule, so outbreak response depends on Centre-State coordination.
Kala-azar is on the WHO neglected tropical disease list, with a 2030 roadmap target of elimination as a public health problem.
stories.mainsQuestion: The reporting of kala-azar from a state outside India's recognised endemic belt raises questions about how disease elimination is defined and verified. Examine the surveillance, federal and socio-economic dimensions of this challenge, and suggest reforms.

stories.headline: Jantar Mantar no longer a protest site; Home Ministry cites national security
stories.summary: The Union Home Ministry has declined to explain why Jantar Mantar in New Delhi is no longer a designated protest site, telling an RTI applicant that disclosure is barred on national security grounds. It also refused to name the authority or individual who recommended the de-notification. The replies, reported by Newslaundry, leave the decision without any public rationale, even though the site has for decades been the capital's principal venue for demonstrations. The episode raises questions about the transparency of executive decisions that restrict assembly and about the widening use of security exemptions under the RTI Act.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the constitutional balance between Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) freedoms and the state's public-order power, and the scope of the national security exemption under the RTI Act — both recurring UPSC themes in GS-II.

perspectives.take: Frames the de-notification as an opaque executive decision, pressing the government on why Jantar Mantar ceased to be a protest site and noting the absence of any public explanation.
Shifts the focus to accountability, highlighting that the government would not reveal who recommended the change and invoked national security to refuse the information.

articles.title: जंतर-मंतर प्रदर्शन स्थल क्यों नहीं रहा? गृह मंत्रालय ने ‘राष्ट्रीय सुरक्षा’ के चलते नहीं बताया
Who suggested de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a protest site? Govt gives no answer, cites national security

static.topic: Right to protest and freedom of assembly
static.syllabusNode: Indian Constitution — Fundamental Rights (Article 19)
static.whatIsIt: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression and Article 19(1)(b) the right to assemble peaceably and without arms; the right to protest is read as a facet of these freedoms, subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2) and 19(3), including on the ground of public order.
static.background: In Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police (1973) the Supreme Court held that public streets are not reserved for traffic alone and that meetings may be regulated but not arbitrarily banned. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018) the Court examined Delhi Police restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar and held that while the police may regulate the time, place and manner of protests, an absolute prohibition is impermissible.
static.geography: Jantar Mantar lies on Parliament Street in central New Delhi, close to Connaught Place and the seat of government.
static.socioEconomic: Concentrating dissent at one designated site affects local residents, businesses and traffic, while channelling citizens' access to the seat of power.
static.whyInNews: The Union Home Ministry has declined to explain, citing national security, the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
static.wayForward: Regulation should be transparent, proportionate and reasoned, with published criteria for designated protest sites and clearly notified alternative venues, so that the public-order power does not become an effective veto on assembly.
keyTerms: Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police (1973)
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018)
prelimsPointers: Article 19(1)(b) guarantees the right to assemble peaceably and without arms; restrictions under Article 19(3) may be imposed on grounds of sovereignty, integrity and public order.
In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) the Supreme Court struck down the absolute prohibition on protests at Jantar Mantar while upholding the police power to regulate them.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the shrinking of designated protest spaces in the capital is compatible with Article 19 and the proportionality standard laid down by the Supreme Court.

static.topic: RTI Act and the national security exemption
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Transparency, Accountability and Right to Information
static.whatIsIt: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives citizens the right to seek information from public authorities; Section 8 lists exempt categories, including Section 8(1)(a) for information affecting national security, and Section 8(2) provides a public-interest override.
static.background: Enacted in 2005 following the MKSS-led transparency movement, the Act established Central and State Information Commissions. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure and salary terms of Information Commissioners. Section 8 exemptions are routinely invoked by ministries to refuse disclosure.
static.socioEconomic: RTI is the principal tool of citizen oversight over the executive; broad use of security exemptions weakens informed public debate and accountability.
static.whyInNews: The Home Ministry refused to disclose who recommended de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a protest site, invoking the national security exemption.
static.wayForward: Exemptions should be applied narrowly with reasons recorded, the public-interest override in Section 8(2) should be actively tested, and the appellate role of the Central Information Commission strengthened.
prelimsPointers: The RTI Act came into force on 12 October 2005; Section 8(1)(a) exempts information prejudicial to national security, sovereignty and integrity.
Section 8(2) permits disclosure where public interest outweighs the harm to the protected interest.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the routine invocation of national security exemptions under the RTI Act affects democratic accountability.

static.topic: Jantar Mantar — heritage monument and public space
static.syllabusNode: Art and Culture — Indian architecture and monuments
static.whatIsIt: Jantar Mantar in New Delhi is an astronomical observatory of masonry instruments built for measuring time and tracking celestial bodies; it is a protected monument under the AMASR Act, 1958.
static.background: Built in 1724 by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur, it is one of a group of observatories he commissioned; the Jaipur Jantar Mantar was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010. The Delhi site has long doubled as a venue for public demonstrations.
static.geography: Located on Parliament Street in central New Delhi, in the vicinity of Connaught Place and government offices.
static.socioEconomic: The monument's precinct became a symbolic space for citizen dissent, and its dual identity as heritage site and protest ground raises questions of urban public-space management.
static.whyInNews: Its de-notification as a designated protest site has renewed debate on heritage precincts and civic space.
static.wayForward: Heritage management and the regulation of public assembly should be reconciled through clearly notified, accessible alternative protest venues.
prelimsPointers: Delhi's Jantar Mantar was built in 1724 by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur.
The Jaipur Jantar Mantar was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010; the Delhi observatory is an ASI-protected monument.
static.mainsAngle: Should heritage precincts in the capital also serve as sites of democratic expression? Discuss with reference to urban public-space governance.

prelims: The Union Home Ministry declined to disclose, citing national security, who recommended de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.
Jantar Mantar in New Delhi has historically been among the sites designated by Delhi Police for public demonstrations.
National security exemptions in the RTI Act are provided under Section 8(1)(a), with a public-interest override in Section 8(2).
stories.mainsQuestion: The right to protest is a facet of the freedom of speech and expression, but it remains subject to reasonable restrictions. In the light of recent restrictions on designated protest sites in the capital, examine the balance between public order and democratic dissent.

stories.headline: Hasina to return to Bangladesh on December 16, says Awami League
stories.summary: The Awami League has said that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina will return to Bangladesh on December 16, a claim that has not been confirmed by the interim government in Dhaka. According to the party, Hasina has asked the Bangladesh government to provide an aircraft for the journey. An Awami League team has also surveyed the Petrapole crossing in West Bengal to assess the Benapole–Petrapole land route, indicating that a return by road is being kept open as an option. The announcement revives a politically charged question in Bangladesh and carries direct implications for India, which hosts Hasina and controls the Indian side of the border infrastructure she may use.
stories.whyItMatters: India's handling of the return of a former ally who is politically contested in Bangladesh tests its stated policy of non-interference in neighbours' internal affairs and its management of a sensitive land border. It is a live case study for GS-II neighbourhood diplomacy and GS-III border management.

perspectives.take: Reports the Awami League's claim as an announcement by the party rather than a confirmed event, and foregrounds the logistics — a requested aircraft and a surveyed land route — signalling that the return plan is still unverified and contingent.

articles.title: Hasina to return to Bangladesh on December 16, says Awami League
articles.snippet: Ousted Prime Minister has asked Bangladesh government for an aircraft; Awami League team has visited Petrapole in West Bengal to assess Benapole-Petrapole crossing in case Ms. Hasina plans to enter Bangladesh trough land border crossing

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh, covering trade, connectivity, water sharing, security cooperation, border management and people-to-people ties, conducted through institutional mechanisms such as the Joint Consultative Commission and regular summit-level exchanges.
static.background: Bangladesh became independent in 1971 with Indian support. The two countries share the world's longest land border for India and have resolved major outstanding issues over time, including the maritime boundary (2014) and the Land Boundary Agreement (2015). Relations deepened during Sheikh Hasina's tenure, and India has since maintained engagement with the interim government in Dhaka.
static.geography: Bangladesh is bounded by India on the west, north and east, with a short border with Myanmar in the southeast and the Bay of Bengal to the south. West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram share borders with Bangladesh.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is a major trade partner and a key source of migrants and labour flows into India; border districts on both sides depend on cross-border trade, transport and informal economic linkages.
static.whyInNews: The Awami League has announced that Sheikh Hasina will return to Bangladesh on December 16, with a party team assessing the Benapole–Petrapole land crossing and a request made for an aircraft.
static.wayForward: India is likely to continue a calibrated approach: upholding its stated position of non-interference in Bangladesh's internal politics while managing border security, trade continuity and the safety of Indian assets and personnel in Bangladesh.
prelimsPointers: India and Bangladesh share a border of over 4,000 km, the longest India shares with any neighbour.
The India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement, operationalised in 2015, exchanged enclaves and simplified the boundary.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how political transitions in neighbouring countries affect India's neighbourhood policy, and discuss the balance India must strike between strategic interests and the principle of non-interference.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Border Management and Land Ports
static.syllabusNode: Security — Border Management
static.whatIsIt: The framework for guarding and facilitating movement across the India–Bangladesh border, involving the Border Security Force, Integrated Check Posts, Land Ports Authority of India and state governments, with a focus on curbing illegal migration, smuggling and trafficking while enabling legal trade.
static.background: Border fencing along the India–Bangladesh frontier has been built in phases, and Integrated Check Posts and land customs stations have been developed to formalise trade. Petrapole, opposite Benapole in Bangladesh, is among the busiest land ports in South Asia and handles a large share of bilateral overland trade.

stories.headline: Courts rule on Bilkis Bano remission, juvenile justice and POCSO cases
stories.summary: A clutch of judicial orders across the country has renewed focus on how Indian courts balance liberty, victim dignity and child protection. In the Bilkis Bano remission matter, the latest order has again left the survivor's quest for justice unresolved, with opinion writers arguing that a convict's right to liberty cannot be allowed to override a survivor's dignity and voice. Separately, commentary on the 2020 Delhi riots cases holds that endless imprisonment without trial raises urgent questions about liberty and the right to a speedy trial. On the juvenile justice side, the Delhi High Court held that the 2021 amendment to the Juvenile Justice Act applies retrospectively and that all affected cases must be moved to the Children's Court, while a Maharashtra Juvenile Justice Board took up the bail plea of a child in conflict with law after the High Court rejected it, citing stunt-riding videos and parental inaction. In parallel, the Madhya Pradesh High Court ruled that holding a minor's hand with sexual intent amounts to sexual assault under POCSO, and a Kerala court's conviction of actor Sreejith T R under the same Act was examined in detail.
stories.whyItMatters: The decisions test the constitutional balance between Article 21 liberty, the right to speedy trial, executive remission powers and the best interests of the child. They are directly relevant to GS-II questions on judicial review, criminal law reform, juvenile justice and child protection.

static.topic: Remission of sentences and judicial review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: Remission is the executive's power to reduce a sentence, exercised under Section 432 of the CrPC (re-enacted in the BNSS, 2023) and state remission policies, but it remains subject to judicial review for arbitrariness and non-application of mind.
static.background: In the Bilkis Bano case arising from the 2002 Gujarat riots, the Supreme Court transferred the trial to Maharashtra, where 11 persons were convicted in 2008. Gujarat granted remission in 2022; in January 2024 the Supreme Court quashed that remission, holding that the appropriate government was Maharashtra and not Gujarat, and directed fresh consideration.
static.geography: Gujarat (place of offence), Maharashtra (place of trial), Supreme Court (Delhi)
static.socioEconomic: Remission decisions in heinous offences raise questions of victim dignity, communal justice and public confidence in the criminal justice system.
static.whyInNews: The latest order in the Bilkis Bano remission matter has again deferred the survivor's quest for justice, prompting fresh debate on executive clemency and victims' rights.
static.wayForward: Codify objective, non-arbitrary remission criteria, mandate a hearing for the victim, ensure that only the appropriate government decides, and strengthen oversight of state remission policies.
prelimsPointers: Under Section 432 CrPC, the 'appropriate government' is the State within which the offender is sentenced.
Remission is distinct from pardon, commutation and reprieve, which are other forms of clemency.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether executive remission powers require statutory guidelines to prevent arbitrariness and to protect the rights of victims.

static.topic: Juvenile Justice Act, Children's Court and retrospective application of amendments
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and Legislative Process; Vulnerable Sections: Children
static.whatIsIt: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 governs children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection, and provides for Juvenile Justice Boards and Children's Courts. The Juvenile Justice (Amendment) Act, 2021 amended it, and the Delhi High Court has now held that the 2021 amendment applies retrospectively, requiring all affected cases to be moved to the Children's Court.
static.background: The JJ Act, 2015 replaced the JJ Act, 2000 in the aftermath of the 2012 Delhi gangrape case and permitted children aged 16-18 accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults after a preliminary assessment by the JJB. The 2021 amendment designated District Magistrates as the authority to issue adoption orders, expanded the definition of 'child in need of care and protection', and enhanced penalties for offences against children.
static.socioEconomic: The framework seeks to balance the best interests of the child with public safety concerns, while parental responsibility and the digital exposure of minors emerge as new challenges.
static.whyInNews: The Delhi High Court ruled that the 2021 amendment is retrospective, and a Maharashtra Juvenile Justice Board heard a child in conflict with law's bail plea after the High Court rejected it, citing stunt-riding videos and parental inaction.
static.wayForward: Ensure timely transfer of cases, build capacity in JJBs and Children's Courts, and prioritise rehabilitation-oriented outcomes over purely punitive responses.

prelimsPointers: The JJ Act, 2015 defines a 'child' as a person below 18 years of age.

static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether India's juvenile justice framework adequately balances the best interests of the child with societal safety, in the light of recent High Court rulings.

static.topic: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012

static.whatIsIt: A gender-neutral special law enacted to protect children below 18 years from sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography, with child-friendly procedures and designated Special Courts.
static.background: POCSO came into force on 14 November 2012. The POCSO Amendment Act, 2019 enhanced punishments, including the death penalty for aggravated penetrative sexual assault, and raised the minimum sentence for such offences. The POCSO Rules, 2020 provide for support persons and compensation for victims.
static.socioEconomic: Courts have progressively widened the interpretation of 'sexual assault' under Section 7, while concerns persist about delayed trials, low conviction rates and inadequate victim rehabilitation.
static.whyInNews: The Madhya Pradesh High Court held that holding a minor's hand with sexual intent amounts to sexual assault under POCSO, and a Kerala court's conviction of actor Sreejith T R under the Act was examined in detail.
static.wayForward: Strengthen Special Courts, victim support and rehabilitation services, and promote consistent judicial interpretation of 'sexual intent' under the Act.
prelimsPointers: POCSO defines a child as any person below 18 years and applies gender-neutrally.
Section 19 mandates reporting of offences under the Act, and failure to report is punishable.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how judicial interpretation of 'sexual intent' under POCSO shapes child protection, and evaluate the implementation challenges facing the Act.

Article 21 has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the right to a speedy trial, enforceable through writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.

stories.headline: US midterm rout reshapes Trump's standing, South America and US-Israel ties
stories.summary: A Democratic "blue wave" in the 2026 US midterm elections has delivered what The New York Times describes as the party's largest House majority in 30 years, following a win in the Tennessee House race, and has visibly weakened President Donald Trump's political position. The fallout is being read far beyond Washington: The Hindu reports that South America is reassessing its far-right alignments after the reported fall of Paraguay's Santiago Peña, whose exit carries weight beyond the country's roughly seven million people. At the same time, a Hindu opinion piece argues that US-Israel relations after the midterms are "strained but not broken". Scroll.in frames the moment as an identity crisis for both parties — Republicans must decide what conservatism now means, Democrats whether liberalism can again be an affirmative project — while Newsweek carries Trump's own midterm strategist on what the GOP must change. Early-vote tracking by NBC News supplies the electoral data underpinning these political readings.
stories.whyItMatters: US midterms are a referendum on the incumbent presidency and often reset the country's foreign-policy bandwidth — directly affecting India's calculus on West Asia, Latin America, trade and diaspora interests. The ideological churn in both American parties is also a live case study for GS-II on comparative constitutions, party systems and the domestic sources of foreign policy.

static.topic: US Midterm Elections and the American Constitutional Design
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Comparative Constitutions; International Relations — Foreign Political Systems
static.whatIsIt: Midterm elections are held in November every two years, at the midpoint of a four-year presidential term. All 435 seats of the House of Representatives and about one-third of the 100-member Senate go to the polls, along with numerous state governorships and legislatures.
static.background: Fixed by the US Constitution (Article I) and the 20th Amendment, midterms have historically functioned as a referendum on the sitting president, with the president's party typically losing seats. They frequently produce 'divided government', where the presidency and one or both chambers are held by different parties, forcing negotiation or gridlock. The 2026 cycle produced a Democratic 'blue wave' and, per The New York Times, the party's largest House majority in 30 years.
static.geography: United States — a federal union of 50 states with a bicameral Congress based in Washington, D.C.
static.socioEconomic: Midterm outcomes are shaped by inflation, cost of living, immigration, abortion and turnout differentials; urban-rural and college/non-college divides increasingly structure both parties' coalitions.
static.whyInNews: The 2026 midterms delivered a decisive Democratic performance, shaking the Trump administration and triggering reassessments within both parties and among US partners abroad.
prelimsPointers: US House of Representatives: 435 members elected for two-year terms; Senate: 100 members with six-year terms, roughly one-third retiring every two years.
The US President is elected for a four-year term through the Electoral College, not by direct popular vote.
Midterms are held in November of the second year of a presidential term and routinely cost the president's party seats.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the US separation-of-powers model, where midterms impose a periodic electoral check, with India's parliamentary system and its instruments of accountability such as the no-confidence motion and anti-defection law.

static.topic: US–Israel Relations and West Asia Policy

static.whatIsIt: The US–Israel 'special relationship' rests on strategic, ideological and domestic-political pillars: large-scale military assistance, intelligence cooperation, diplomatic cover at the UN Security Council, and the influence of pro-Israel constituencies in American politics.
static.background: The US recognised Israel in 1948, shortly after its establishment. Israel was designated a Major Non-NATO Ally in 1987, and assistance is institutionalised through ten-year memoranda of understanding, including the 2016 MoU providing $38 billion over a decade. Relations have periodically seen friction over settlements, the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) and US votes at the UN. India recognised Israel in 1950 and established full diplomatic relations in 1992.
static.geography: Israel is a small Levantine state on the eastern Mediterranean; its location at the junction of West Asia, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea corridor gives it strategic salience.
static.socioEconomic: US aid and arms transfers underpin Israel's defence industrial and technological base; domestic lobbies, evangelical constituencies and campaign finance make Israel policy electorally salient in the US.
static.whyInNews: A Hindu opinion piece argues that US–Israel ties after the midterm results are 'strained but not broken', as a changed Washington reassesses its regional posture.
prelimsPointers: Israel was designated a Major Non-NATO Ally of the United States in 1987.
The US has repeatedly used its UN Security Council veto on resolutions concerning Israel.
India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992, though recognition dates to 1950.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how domestic political transitions in the United States reshape its West Asia policy, and evaluate the implications for India's balancing act between Israel, the Gulf states and Iran.

static.topic: South America's Political Swing and India–Latin America Ties

static.whatIsIt: South America has experienced repeated pendulum swings between left and right governments, mediated through regional groupings such as Mercosur, CELAC and the Pacific Alliance, and through the Organisation of American States (OAS).
static.background: The 'pink tide' of the 2000s brought left-wing governments to Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela and Bolivia, giving way to right-wing turns in Argentina (2015) and Brazil (2018), followed by left returns in Argentina (2019), Chile (2021), Colombia (2022) and Brazil (2022). Mercosur was created by the 1991 Treaty of Asunción among Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Paraguay, a landlocked country of about seven million people, is the only Mercosur member that recognises Taiwan rather than the People's Republic of China.
static.geography: South America — a continent of twelve sovereign states, dominated demographically and economically by Brazil; Paraguay is landlocked, with its capital at Asunción.
static.socioEconomic: Commodity dependence, inequality, migration pressures and Chinese infrastructure lending are the principal socio-economic drivers of Latin American political volatility.
static.whyInNews: The Hindu reports that after Trump's midterm rout, South America is breathing easier and its far right is under pressure, with the reported fall of Paraguay's Santiago Peña cited as evidence of a wider regional shift.

Mercosur was established by the 1991 Treaty of Asunción with Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay as founding members.
India's engagement with Latin America runs through mechanisms such as the India–CELAC dialogue and IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa).
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political volatility in Latin America affects India's energy security, food security and market diversification strategies, and suggest how India can deepen its Global South outreach.

onThisDay.title: Anti-Comintern Pact signed

onThisDay.title: Mirabal sisters assassinated
onThisDay.description: The Mirabal sisters of the Dominican Republic were assassinated under the Trujillo dictatorship. Their deaths later inspired the UN designation of November 25 as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.
onThisDay.upscLink: Social Justice: gender-based violence, women's rights.

onThisDay.title: Jeddah floods during Hajj
onThisDay.description: Freak rains caused severe flooding in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, during the Hajj pilgrimage, sweeping away thousands of cars and killing at least 122 people. The disaster highlighted urban flooding risks in arid regions and pilgrimage safety challenges.
onThisDay.upscLink: Disaster Management: urban flooding, Hajj pilgrimage safety.

onThisDay.title: Czechoslovakia votes to split
onThisDay.description: The Federal Assembly of Czechoslovakia voted to dissolve the country into the Czech Republic and Slovakia, effective January 1, 1993. This peaceful separation became known as the Velvet Divorce.
